source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox
finding: Three-stage history. Field studies of decisions in the 1980s (Rasmussen, Cohen, Beach and Mitchell, Klein, Noble) became Naturalistic Decision Making (NDM) at a 1989 workshop. NDM widened to macrocognition in 2003. Then models were turned into methods and tools.
numbers: About 30 researchers at the 1989 workshop; book Decision Making in Action (Klein et al. 1993); 12 NDM conferences held by 2016; Human Factors and Ergonomics Society technical group since 1995.
limits: Written by the founders (Klein is lead author). A perspective piece, not a neutral review.
agent_relevance: Macrocognition is a research stance (study thinking where the work is done) more than one theory. For us it is a source of tested functions to copy, not a spec.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox
finding: The recognition-primed decision (RPD) model is the founding result. Experienced people under time pressure often do not compare options. They recognise the situation, take the first workable action, and check it by mental simulation.
numbers: Authors say RPD accounted for 80-90% of firefighter decisions (Klein et al. 1986; Klein 1989). Cited replications: military leaders (Schmitt and Klein 1999), firefighters in virtual reality (Keren et al. 2013), offshore oil platform managers (Skriver 1998); tests by Klein et al. 1995 and Johnson and Raab 2003.
quote: The RPD model accounted for 80-90% of the decisions that firefighters made.
limits: The 80-90% figure is the founders' own summary; the replications are cited, not reread. The discovery needs 10-20 years of experience, so novices do not show it.
agent_relevance: Maps to a cheap first-option route (propose one candidate, check it) with comparison only after a failed check. An LLM has no 10-20 years of tacit patterns but has broad pattern knowledge, so this is plausible, not proven.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox
finding: The founders list beliefs NDM says are wrong: you must generate several options and compare; expertise is rules; projects need a clear goal; sensemaking builds up from data to knowledge; insight needs overcoming mental sets; more information reduces uncertainty; teaching critical-thinking precepts such as listing assumptions improves performance.
numbers: Seven 'no longer believe' claims, each with citations (information: Omodei et al. 2005, Flin et al. 2008, Grossman et al. 2014; assumptions: Klein 2011, Hoffman et al. 2014).
quote: experienced personnel use their mental models to define what counts as data in the first place
limits: Claims by the founders, many resting on case studies. 'More information does not reduce uncertainty' is a finding that performance fell when too much was gathered, so it is condition-bound.
agent_relevance: Supports G1 (no scheduled doubt) and the point that listing assumptions on a schedule is weak. Gathering more data is not a fix by itself; framing matters.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox
finding: Macrocognition was defined against microcognition. Macro: firefighters, pilots, nurses facing hard dilemmas under time pressure and uncertainty. Micro: components such as working memory and serial versus parallel attention. The founders say macrocognition cares less about hypothesis tests and precision, more about useful descriptive models and plausibility.
numbers: Definition from Klein, Klein and Klein (2000); the term was used earlier by Cacciabue and Hollnagel (1995). Functions figure from Klein et al. (2003).
quote: It is less concerned with testing hypotheses than with formulating useful models and theories.
limits: The founders concede the criticisms (no correct answers, hard to score) and say 'guilty as charged'. That is a methods limit, not a rebuttal.
agent_relevance: Our evaluation needs scored tasks, so macrocognitive claims need a measurable check. Treat the models as hypotheses to test.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox
finding: Critics inside decision research objected. Lipshitz et al. (2001) in the Journal of Behavioral Decision Making drew 16 commentaries asking NDM to mature with more controlled methods. NDM answered that controlled studies would no longer be NDM. Naturalistic Memory (Neisser) faded after a special issue attacking it (Banaji and Crowder 1989).
numbers: 16 commentaries on Lipshitz et al. 2001.
limits: Account is from the NDM side only.
agent_relevance: The descriptive, non-normative stance has been contested for 25 years; weigh RPD claims against lab work.

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox
finding: Stage-3 tools: a railway case shows a macrocognitive diagnosis. Drivers passing signals at danger were not simply inattentive: the red light was always lit so it carried no information, stations had outgrown their layout, and trains were so long that signals could sit behind the cab.
numbers: Case: Multer et al. (2015); Safar et al. (2015). No effect size. Holtrop et al. (2015): two-day CTA workshop for care outreach staff judged 'highly successful' (no numbers).
limits: Single case narratives; no controlled outcome numbers in the paper.
agent_relevance: Fix the frame or display before blaming the actor. When the agent errs, check whether the input format (prompt, tool output) misled it before adding doubt steps (G2).

source: Klein & Wright (2016) Macrocognition: From Theory to Toolbox
finding: ShadowBox is a training tool: a trainee ranks options at decision points and writes a rationale, then sees a pooled expert ranking and rationale. Five uses: training, expert-knowledge capture, assessment, teamwork prediction, leadership calibration.
numbers: Originated by Hintze (2008); elaborated Klein et al. (2013). No effect size in this paper.
limits: No measured outcome in this source.
agent_relevance: A held-out expert-ranking comparison could be an offline check for scaffold steps (scored in code, not by a model judge).

source: Ward et al. (2017) Editorial: Macrocognition (Frontiers Research Topic)
finding: The 2017 Frontiers editorial defines macrocognition as how cognition adapts to complexity in work, studied with cognitive task analysis that mixes naturalistic and experimental methods, aiming at work-as-done rather than work-as-prescribed.
numbers: Seven authors; 11 articles in the Research Topic; received 2017-03-01, accepted 2017-03-21.
quote: Macrocognition has evolved as a complementary paradigm, focused on how cognition adapts to complexity
limits: Editorial: summaries, not primary data.
agent_relevance: Our scaffold is 'work-as-prescribed'. Macrocognition predicts a gap between this and what the model does; log real traces to see it.

source: Ward et al. (2017) Editorial: Macrocognition (Frontiers Research Topic)
finding: Editorial reports: experienced operators can supervise about 15 unmanned systems at moderate automation but control only about three well, and teams generally beat individuals (Porat et al.).
numbers: About 15 supervised versus up to 3 controlled; teams better than individuals 'generally'.
limits: Second-hand from the editorial; the team result need not transfer to one agent.
agent_relevance: The number of items one agent can actively steer is small. Argues for few concurrent hypotheses or tool threads in the state machine.

source: Ward et al. (2017) Editorial: Macrocognition (Frontiers Research Topic)
finding: Editorial: sending many messages can lower the chance of shared situation awareness (Buchler et al.), and similarity of team members' roles and starting awareness mattered.
numbers: Qualitative; no figures in the editorial.
limits: Team/network result; second-hand.
agent_relevance: More output (messages, samples) is not more shared understanding. Keep inter-component messages to compact state (G4, G5 flavour).

source: Ward et al. (2017) Editorial: Macrocognition (Frontiers Research Topic)
finding: Editorial summary of two NDM field studies: sports coaches use deliberation as a quick check on first intuitions (Collins et al.), and police gather, frame and share information to coordinate incident response (Baber and McMaster).
numbers: Qualitative.
quote: deliberation is often used as an immediate check on initial intuitions
limits: Second-hand; see the coach interview study (a16).
agent_relevance: 'Intuition then a short check' matches our propose-then-verify loop.

source: Ward et al. (2017) Editorial: Macrocognition (Frontiers Research Topic)
finding: Editorial notes a critique by Laurent and Bianchi: macrocognition may not need to be separated from other cognition; micro and macro are levels of analysis, and a multiscale model is needed where context and cognition interact at several levels.
numbers: One critical paper among 11.
limits: Critique as summarised by the editors.
agent_relevance: Warns against treating the macro/micro split as a mechanism.

source: Laurent & Bianchi (2016) Macrocognition through the Multiscale Enaction Model lens
finding: Critical paper arguing macrocognition has a blind spot: motivated or need-driven cognition. Proposes the Multiscale Enaction Model. Only the keywords and reference list were visible to me.
numbers: Keywords: complexity, enaction, motivated cognition, multiscale cognition, needs. Published 2016-07-27.
limits: Not read in full; the body text was not retrievable this session.
agent_relevance: Low direct use. Marks that the field's theory is contested on what 'macro' means.

source: Brouwers, Wiggins, Helton, O'Hare & Griffin (2016) Cue utilization and cognitive load in novel task performance, Experiment 1
finding: In a 20-minute simulated rail control task (67 trains), people with high cue utilisation (from the EXPERTise tests) were slower but as accurate as low-cue people. Cue use looked like a way to save effort, not to go faster.
numbers: N=58 (34 low, 24 high). Mean latency high 2079.7 ms (SD 395.7) vs low 1527.4 ms (SD 498.6); F(1,56)=20.36, p<.001, eta2=.267. Errors 0-5 per person, median 1; 64% made 0 or 1 error. Driving experience equal (38.2 vs 39.5 months, p=.77).
limits: Novel lab micro-world; cue utilisation is a trait measure; no accuracy difference; group-by-block interaction not significant, F=1.09, p=.349.
agent_relevance: Fast pattern use is not what marked expertise here; steady, lower-load work did. Do not reward speed alone when scoring macrocognitive-style steps.

source: Brouwers et al. (2016) Cue utilization and cognitive load, Experiment 2
finding: A concurrent secondary task slowed low-cue people more than high-cue people. High-cue people kept response times steady across blocks despite added load.
numbers: N=55 (22 low, 33 high). Manipulation check on 5 volunteers: dual-task latency 3063 ms vs 2691 ms single-task. Interaction reported by authors; I did not extract its F value.
limits: Small N; secondary task was writing train number and time on paper; one simulation.
agent_relevance: Stored cue knowledge shields against load. For an LLM, loaded context may hurt weakly-patterned tasks more; test with distractor context.

source: Collins, Collins & Carson (2016) 'If it feels right, do it': intuitive decision making in high-level sport coaches (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Interview study of 18 coaches (10 adventure-sport, 8 rugby union). All said they use intuitive decisions in practice, more as experience grew, often as the first call in live sessions or games.
numbers: N=18; theme 'Aspects of decision making process' in 10/10 adventure and 8/8 rugby coaches; 'Audit (change of perspective on decision making)' in 8/10 and 8/8.
limits: Self-report interviews; two sports; no performance outcome.
agent_relevance: Self-report of intuition is weak evidence of mechanism; do not read a model's written rationale as how it decided (schema section 1).

source: Klein, Moon & Hoffman (2006) Making sense of sensemaking 2: a macrocognitive model (IEEE Intelligent Systems 21:88-92)
finding: Data-frame model of sensemaking. A frame is a story or map that defines what counts as data, and data in turn shape the frame. Sensemaking cycles through connecting data to a frame, elaborating, questioning, preserving, comparing frames, re-framing and seeking a new frame.
numbers: Not read directly. The core flow (starts when someone questions a frame; tracking anomalies, inconsistencies, plausibility, data quality) is confirmed in the 2023 paper (a18).
limits: Not opened; the model rests on case studies, no effect sizes. Fuller account: Klein et al. (2007) chapter 'A data-frame theory of sensemaking'.
agent_relevance: Template for state transitions: hold one frame, test for anomalies, reframe only on a signal. Matches G1.

source: Hoffman, Klein et al. (2023) The plausibility transition model for sensemaking (Frontiers in Psychology)
finding: Story-building model of sensemaking built from 23 cases. A surprise triggers a story. Each state-to-state step is judged for plausibility. Gaps are filled with assumptions. If anomalies grow, confidence drops and a new story is built ('snap-back').
numbers: 23 cases taken from a corpus of 73 (Klein et al. 2021); examples: Air France 447, USS Vincennes, AlphaGo, Royal Majesty grounding; one reviewer (the senior author) analysed them.
quote: the explanation process of story-building is triggered by surprises and anomalies
limits: Convenience sample, single coder, no reliability figure, no test of predictions. The authors call it exploratory.
agent_relevance: The anomaly count is a usable trigger: doubt grows as unexplained items accumulate (a code-counted signal, G1). Count unexplained facts rather than ask the model if the story feels plausible.

source: Hoffman, Klein et al. (2023) plausibility transition model, Data/Frame restatement
finding: Data/Frame model restated: sensemaking starts when someone questions an existing frame; plausibility matters both for elaborating a frame and for seeking a new one. Explaining away gets harder as anomalies pile up, which pushes people to switch frames.
numbers: Figure 1 of the paper, adapted from Klein et al. (2007). No numeric tests.
limits: Descriptive.
agent_relevance: Gives a concrete re-framing rule: switch when the cost of explaining away passes a threshold.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026) Intuition and deliberation in elite expertise (Cognitive Research: Principles and Implications), Study 1
finding: Boundary condition on the RPD emphasis: elite chess players made more and bigger blunders under high time pressure (blitz), so intuition alone did not carry expertise. They used time strategically, intuiting when feasible and deliberating when needed.
numbers: Study 1: 20 grandmasters, 104 pairs of games, standard vs blitz. Blunder proportion t(19)=6.54, d=1.39; blunder size t(19)=4.23, d=0.96, both p<.001; mean blunder about half a pawn larger in blitz. Expected blunder per move: t(19)=-5.79, d=1.30. Engine: Fritz 9.0 Blundercheck.
quote: Time pressure should have minimal effects on expert performance if intuitive processes are the primary basis
limits: Archival chess; closed, rule-bound domain; blunder is engine-defined; targets the intuition emphasis, not RPD's simulation step.
agent_relevance: Let the program grant more deliberation when budget allows; do not trust one fast pass. Fits budgeted use of operators.

source: Vidulich & Tsang (2026), Study 2 and framing of RPD
finding: Study 2 used 7 world champions and found the same pattern: as game circumstances forced fast moves, blunder propensity rose, and some fast moves were big blunders. The paper quotes Klein (2015, p.165) that experienced people rarely choose among options and take the first they consider.
numbers: Study 2: 7 world champions (N from the abstract). Effect sizes for Study 2 not extracted.
limits: RPD itself includes a mental-simulation step; the critique targets how applied work stresses intuition.
agent_relevance: Keep the 'simulate before commit' half of RPD, not only the first-option half.

source: Cognitive task analysis of resident physician fluid-resuscitation decisions in the ICU (2025, PMC12712819)
finding: Critical decision method interviews coded with the RPD model as the frame. Residents' fluid decisions rested on intuition and volume heuristics (e.g. over 3-5 L will not help) even where evidence-based predictors existed; premature closure, confirmation bias and status-quo bias appeared.
numbers: 11 of 23 eligible residents interviewed; median 7 days (IQR 6.5-11) from event to interview; seven domains: cues, information, decision making, alternatives, analogs, expected outcomes, goals.
limits: 11 interviewees, one hospital, week-old recall, no outcome measure.
agent_relevance: RPD-style matching can lock in a heuristic. Shows why a first guess needs a held-out check (G3) even when it feels recognised.

source: Norwegian Armed Forces survey of Klein's decision-making claims (2026, PMC13113691)
finding: Military professionals did not hold Klein's claims as one belief. Factor analysis found two: Planning/Structure and Analytic/Evidence-based practice. Endorsement is split, not unified.
numbers: N=225 (177 men, 48 women; mean age 25.9); 11 items, 2 dropped; KMO=.741; Bartlett chi2(36)=282.86; two factors explain 29.24% of variance; alpha .65 and .71; top loadings .618 and .556.
limits: Young convenience sample at a defence college; measures beliefs, not decisions; low variance explained.
agent_relevance: The NDM-versus-analytic debate is not either-or even for practitioners. A scaffold should blend structure with pattern use.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng)
finding: First direct test of NDM prompts on LLMs. Prompts telling a model to reason by recognition-primed decision making or by data-frame theory raised mean accuracy on 45 real care-seeking vignettes across 10 ChatGPT models.
numbers: 13,500 assessments (10 models x 45 vignettes x 3 prompts x 10 runs). Accuracy: default 63.3% (CI 61.9-64.7), recognition-primed 67.6% (66.3-69), data-frame 66.7% (65.3-68). Odds ratio 2.26 (RPD, z=8.69) and 2.05 (data-frame, z=7.23), both p<.001.
limits: One domain (triage advice), one vendor's chat models, vignettes not live cases; the authors call it a technical evaluation, not clinical validation.
agent_relevance: Positive but modest, about +4 points. Evidence that framing prompts shift behaviour. Test a code-checked version on our own tasks; we have no triage data.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng)
finding: Gains were concentrated in one class. Self-care accuracy rose from 13.4% (default) to 29.8% (RPD prompt) and 24.6% (data-frame prompt). Nonemergency stayed near 82% and emergency near 98-100%. Non-reasoning models that never gave self-care advice began to.
numbers: Self-care: 13.4% (CI 11.6-15.4) vs 29.8% (27.3-32.3) vs 24.6% (22.3-27.1). Nonemergency 82.5 / 82.0 / 82.8%. Emergency only 2 vignettes. GPT-4.1 self-care 0% to 43.8% (RPD) and 39.2% (data-frame). 88% of all errors were over-triage.
limits: The prompt may mainly have shifted the decision threshold (less over-triage) rather than improved reasoning; 2 emergency cases so no safety claim.
agent_relevance: The effect looks like recalibration of a bias. Check any scaffold gain against a plain threshold shift before crediting the reasoning.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng)
finding: Per-model results are mixed. Largest gain: GPT-4.1 mini with data-frame prompt, +13 points (49.8% to 62.4%). The newest models gained little or lost: GPT-5.2 Instant 57.8% to 56.4% (RPD) and 55.3% (data-frame); GPT-5.2 Thinking 52.0% to 53.1% and 51.8%.
numbers: Per case, the RPD prompt raised accuracy in 18 of 45 vignettes (40%, median +18%) and lowered it in 13 (29%, median -5%). Data-frame: up in 17 (38%), down in 12 (27%). 92% of decreases were nonemergency cases. Reasoning models gained more (OR 2.15 RPD, p<.001; OR 1.70 data-frame, p=.008).
limits: Most single-model CIs overlap; prompts cost extra output tokens.
agent_relevance: The gain shrinks or vanishes in some models and about three in ten cases got worse. A candidate, not a settled operator; judge by per-item checks, not average accuracy.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng)
finding: Robustness: the result held with binary care versus self-care coding and at low temperature. Output variability was similar across the three prompts.
numbers: Tables S1, S2, S4 in the appendix (not read). Each combination run 10 times.
limits: Appendix tables not opened.
agent_relevance: Run-to-run variability was not reduced, so the prompt is not a variance control.

source: Kopka & Feufel (2026) Increasing LLM accuracy for care-seeking advice using prompts reflecting human reasoning strategies (JMIR Biomed Eng)
finding: Authors' stated limits: one benchmark in one domain, 2 emergency vignettes, only ChatGPT-integrated models, prompts add reasoning output and cost, no human users tested.
numbers: Cost: extra tokens per query.
limits: The authors' own limits.
agent_relevance: Weigh token cost before adopting RPD or data-frame steps; do not generalise to puzzle tasks like ARC.

source: Klein, Calderwood & Clinton-Cirocco (1986) Rapid decision making on the fire ground (Proc. Human Factors Society 30:576-580; DTIC ADA199492 report 1988)
finding: Founding field study: fireground commanders were interviewed about real incidents. They said they seldom compared options; they recognised the situation as typical and acted. This led to RPD. Not opened this session (DTIC returned 403).
numbers: Exact N and share not confirmed this session. Use the 80-90% figure that Klein and Wright (2016) report (a02).
limits: Retrospective interviews; no control group; researchers coded the incidents.
agent_relevance: Treat exact N and percentages as unconfirmed until the 1986 or 1988 report is read.

source: Johnson & Raab (2003) Take the first: option-generation and resulting choices (Org. Behav. Hum. Decis. Processes 91:215-229)
finding: Lab test of RPD's claim that the first option an expert generates tends to be good and more options do not help. Cited by Klein and Wright (2016) as support. Not opened.
numbers: No numbers confirmed this session.
limits: Only the citation was read; the task is sports video scenes, not open-ended field decisions.
agent_relevance: If it holds, a plain first answer plus a check can beat broad option lists. Verify before relying on it.

source: Lipshitz, Klein, Orasanu & Salas (2001) Taking stock of naturalistic decision making (J. Behav. Decis. Making 14:331-352)
finding: The main review of NDM, answered by 16 commentaries. Not opened; only its existence and the commentary count (from a05) are confirmed.
numbers: 16 commentaries (from Klein and Wright 2016).
limits: Paywalled; not read.
agent_relevance: Read it before claiming NDM models were validated.

source: Kahneman & Klein (2009) Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree (American Psychologist 64:515-526)
finding: Joint paper of the heuristics-and-biases and NDM camps. Not opened (PubMed and APA blocked). Remembered core claim, unverified here: intuition is trustworthy only in a regular environment with enough practice and feedback to learn its cues.
numbers: No numbers. DOI confirmed by a Crossref lookup.
limits: Not read; the content is from memory.
agent_relevance: The main boundary condition for any 'trust the first pattern' step; add a task-validity check (links to the Task-type limits subfield).
